facts.claim: Opie and Tatem's A Dictionary of Superstitions (Oxford University Press) gives the earliest dated citation for the rhyme as Charlotte Burne's Shropshire Folk-Lore (1883, page 290), which records it as the saying of 'some Lancashire friends': 'Something old, something new, Something borrowed, and something blue.'
facts.quote: 1883 BURNE Shropshire 290. The dictum of some Lancashire friends … is, 'Something old, something new, Something borrowed, and something blue.'
facts.conflicts: Read via Oxford Reference publisher abstract/search excerpt (full entry behind subscription), Apify web-fetch 2026-11-09. | CONFLICT: the pillar pack (wedding-traditions fact_14) cites St James's Magazine 1871 via phrases.org.uk; not verified in any scan this run (archive.org 1871 volume search errored). Two Oxford references give 1883 as the first record. [[VERIFY: St James's Magazine 1871 printing against a scan before any 1871 date is stated]]

facts.claim: Simpson and Roud's A Dictionary of English Folklore (Oxford) calls 'Something old, something new, something borrowed, something blue' the widest-known wedding rhyme today and says it was first recorded in Shropshire only in 1883 (Burne, 1883: 290).
facts.quote: The widest-known rhyme today is 'Something old, something new, something borrowed, something blue', first recorded in Shropshire only in 1883 ( Burne , 1883 : 290).
facts.conflicts: Read via Oxford Reference publisher abstract/search excerpt (full entry behind subscription), Apify web-fetch 2026-11-09.

facts.claim: Burne (1883), as quoted by Opie and Tatem, records that when the wedding gown was white, the 'blue' was carried by making the garters blue.
facts.quote: When the wedding gown is of the orthodox white, the obligation to wear 'blue' is carried out by making the garters of that colour.
facts.conflicts: Read via Oxford Reference publisher abstract/search excerpt (full entry behind subscription), Apify web-fetch 2026-11-09.

facts.claim: Opie and Tatem quote Folklore (1957, p. 416): the four items were 'almost always worn, even by the most sophisticated brides'.
facts.quote: 1957 Folklore 416. 'Something old, something new, something borrowed and something blue' is almost always worn, even by the most sophisticated brides.
facts.conflicts: Read via Oxford Reference publisher abstract/search excerpt (full entry behind subscription), Apify web-fetch 2026-11-09.

facts.claim: Opie and Tatem's entry on 'something borrowed' cites Henderson's Northern Counties (1866, p. 35): the bride should wear something borrowed, with no reason given.
facts.quote: 1866 HENDERSON Northern Counties 35. The bride … should wear something borrowed—for what reason I am not informed.
facts.conflicts: Read via Oxford Reference publisher abstract/search excerpt (full entry behind subscription), Apify web-fetch 2026-11-09. | Entry 'BRIDE'S CLOTHES: something borrowed' read only in the Oxford Reference search excerpt; entry URL not captured.

facts.claim: Burne (1883, p. 289), as quoted by Opie and Tatem, says it was widely thought lucky to wear something on the wedding day already worn by a happy bride.
facts.quote: it is widely accounted 'lucky' to wear something on the wedding day which has already been worn by a happy bride at her...
facts.conflicts: Read via Oxford Reference publisher abstract/search excerpt (full entry behind subscription), Apify web-fetch 2026-11-09.

facts.claim: Simpson and Roud say many hold that the borrowed item should be something worn at a previous wedding whose marriage turned out happily, and that the veil is often singled out as the luckiest.
facts.quote: Many say the item borrowed should be something worn at a previous wedding, provided the marriage turned out happily; the veil is often singled out as the luckiest.
facts.conflicts: Read via Oxford Reference publisher abstract/search excerpt (full entry behind subscription), Apify web-fetch 2026-11-09.

facts.claim: Simpson and Roud say blue is associated with loyalty and true love and hence lucky for brides; the saying 'Marry in blue, Your love will be true' comes from the blue/true rhyme, noticed from the Middle Ages, and Chaucer calls blue a sign of the 'trouthe' (faithfulness) seen in women.
facts.quote: a colour associated with loyalty and true love, and hence lucky for brides, who must wear: Something old, something new, Something borrowed, something blue. In the days when bridal dresses were not necessarily white, blue was a good colour to choose: Marry in blue, Your love will be true. This meaning is derived from the rhyme 'blue/true', which has been noticed from the Middle Ages onwards; Chaucer refers to blue drapery as a 'signe of trouthe that is in wommen sene'
facts.conflicts: Read via Oxford Reference publisher abstract/search excerpt (full entry behind subscription), Apify web-fetch 2026-11-09.

facts.claim: Opie and Tatem's entry 'something blue' records blue being recommended as the lucky colour for a wedding dress, and a 1988 mother of the bride (St Albans) mentioning 'the blue garter of course'.
facts.quote: Her seniors, all … recommended blue as the lucky colour [for her wedding dress]. 1988 [St Albans, Herts.] 'This is my daughter's wedding dress,' she said, and added with a little giggle, 'And the blue garter of course.'
facts.conflicts: Read via Oxford Reference publisher abstract/search excerpt (full entry behind subscription), Apify web-fetch 2026-11-09.

facts.quote: 1946 Mirror 29 Aug. 6 . 'Something old, Something new, Something borrowed, Something blue, And a silver sixpence In your shoe'

facts.claim: Opie and Tatem quote Sean O'Casey's I Knock at the Door (set in Dublin): a bride 'having with her something old and something new, something borrowed and something blue, and a lucky sixpence in her shoe'.
facts.quote: S. O'CASEY I Knock at the Door 103 [Dublin] [On her wedding morning] she was ready for any emergency, so she was, having with her something old and something new, something borrowed and something blue, and a lucky sixpence in her shoe.

facts.claim: Simpson and Roud note a silver sixpence is frequently mentioned as a lucky charm, especially in a bride's shoe.
facts.quote: A silver sixpence is frequently mentioned: as a gift to a new baby ; as a gift left by fairies for diligent servant girls, or for children shedding a tooth ; as a lucky charm , especially in a bride's shoe

facts.claim: Smartraveller (updated 18 August 2026): travel insurance can cover replacing baggage and valuables if lost, damaged or stolen; policies often limit each item's value, so check individual item limits and whether extra cover for valuables is needed.
facts.quote: Travel insurance can cover replacing your baggage and valuables if they're lost, damaged or stolen. ... Policies vary when it comes to how they cover valuable items. They often limit each item's value.
facts.conflicts: Reuses engagement-ring-insurance fact_13, re-checked live 2026-11-09; page also mentions a dollar range for valuables cover, deliberately not recorded (no amounts).

facts.claim: Smartraveller: always read the Product Disclosure Statement (PDS) before buying a policy, and declare everything upfront or you may void it; insurance will rarely cover theft of items left unattended.
facts.quote: Always read the Product Disclosure Statement (PDS) before you buy a policy. ... Always declare everything upfront when you buy your policy. If you don't, you may void it. ... Insurance will also rarely cover: the theft of items you left unattended

facts.claim: Smartraveller theft page (updated 18 August 2026): standard travel policies typically don't cover loss of items left unattended, items not stored in a hotel safe when one was available, items stolen from checked baggage on an airline, train or bus, or losses without a police report.
facts.quote: Standard travel insurance policies typically don't cover the loss of items if: they were left unattended; you did not store them in a hotel safe when one was available; ... you don't get a police report proving your loss; ... your items were stolen from a locked car or checked baggage on an airline, train or bus.

facts.claim: Smartraveller theft page: before you go, consider leaving expensive items at home; while away, think about leaving valuables in the hotel safe, keep belongings and bags close in transit, and keep valuables out of sight.
facts.quote: Consider leaving expensive items at home. ... Think about leaving valuables in the hotel safe rather than taking them out with you. Keep your belongings and bags close when exploring or in transit. Insurance usually won't cover unattended items. ... Keep money and valuables out of sight.

facts.quote: Sarah Maria Wright (1817 – 1908) wore this dress for her marriage to Daniel Neal (1816 – 1907) on 27 July 1841 at St. Nicholas' Church in Skirbeck, Lincolnshire. ... Historical significance: This dress is a rare example of a dress chosen by a working-class bride for her wedding.

facts.claim: V&A T.27-2006: the V&A says dresses like this survive in smaller numbers than fashionable wedding dresses because they were worn as Sunday best long after the wedding, or handed down; the bodice has been carefully enlarged (gallery label: '1841, with later alterations').
facts.quote: Such objects tend to survive in much smaller quantities than fashionable wedding dress as they would have been worn for Sunday best long after the event, or handed down. ... The bodice has been carefully enlarged.

insider_details.detail: Quote the rhyme in the Burne 1883 four-line form and present the sixpence line separately with its 1946 Mirror printing, so every dated version on the page traces to a citation.

For something borrowed, the documented custom is to borrow from a happily married bride, often her veil; an Advisor can suggest asking a married sister, friend or mother early so the piece can be cleaned and fitted.
Something blue has long been worn out of sight (the blue garter), which suits couples who want the tradition without changing the palette.
The sixpence goes in the left shoe; for a destination wedding it is a small coin worth packing in hand luggage with the other heirloom pieces.

Carry heirlooms and jewellery on your person or in hand luggage, never in checked bags: Smartraveller lists items stolen from checked baggage among common travel-insurance exclusions, and most policies won't pay for items left unattended.

Before flying, photograph every piece (the brooch, the borrowed earrings, the ring) and keep valuations or proof of ownership with your travel documents, because insurers may ask for them at claim time.

Read the travel policy's PDS for per-item limits and declare valuable pieces upfront; a borrowed family piece is still something you are carrying, so check whether it needs specified cover or sits under the owner's contents policy (see /style-advice/engagement-ring-insurance).

At the venue, use the in-room or hotel safe between the ceremony and reception events; Smartraveller notes standard policies often exclude losses when a hotel safe was available and not used, and claims need a local police report.

A wedding dress that is altered, re-worn or handed down has a long museum pedigree: the V&A holds an 1841 cotton wedding dress with a carefully enlarged bodice, and notes such dresses were worn as Sunday best or handed down. That is a natural frame for re-cutting a mother's dress or lace as 'something old'.

Blue in a wedding outfit need not be a garter: the V&A's 1841 dress is white cotton printed with blue among its colours, and the V&A notes many brides wore practical coloured dresses. A blue thread or print in fabric reads as considered, not novelty.
